claims.claim: For the network to behave as an autoassociative memory, it needs to be able to store and dynamically retrieve multiple manifolds.
claims.source: We described in detail the behavior of a neural network with asymmetric connectivity in the case of a single manifold encoded in the synaptic connectivity. For the network to behave as an autoassociative memory, however, it needs to be able to store and dynamically retrieve multiple manifolds.
claims.evidence: Logical requirement for memory function.

claims.claim: The resulting dynamics show multiple continuous attractors corresponding to the stored manifolds.
claims.source: The resulting dynamics show multiple continuous attractors, corresponding to the stored manifolds.
claims.evidence: Result from the multi-manifold model.

claims.claim: Given an initial configuration, the network rapidly converges to the nearest attractor, forming a coherent bump that then moves along the manifold.
claims.source: Given an initial configuration, the networks rapidly converges to the nearest (i.e. most correlated) attractor, forming a coherent bump that then moves along the manifold as a consequence of the asymmetric component of the connectivity.
claims.evidence: Description of network behavior with multiple manifolds.

claims.claim: The same dynamics, if projected on unretrieved manifolds, appear as random noise.
claims.source: The same dynamics, if projected on the other unretrieved manifolds, appear as random noise.
claims.evidence: Result from simulations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: When cells are sorted according to their firing field on the retrieved manifold, they show sequential activity.
claims.source: When ordered as in the retrieved manifold, the recorded cells show a structured pattern that is considered the hallmark of sequential activity in experimental studies (Figure 6c, first column).
claims.evidence: Result from simulated recording shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: When spikes are ordered according to unretrieved manifolds, the sequential pattern is lost.
claims.source: If the same spikes are ordered according to the unretrieved manifolds, the pattern is lost (Figure 6c, second and third column), indicating that the population activity is retrieving the dynamical structure of the first manifold specifically.
claims.evidence: Result from simulated recording shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: Multiple dynamic manifolds can be memorized and retrieved by the network with different speeds.
claims.source: Multiple dynamic manifolds can be memorized and retrieved by the network, with different speeds.
claims.evidence: Result from simulations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Manifolds are dynamically retrieved at different speeds depending on the corresponding γ.
claims.source: Figure 7 (b) shows the result of the numerical simulation of a network with five different one-dimensional manifold stored in its connectivity matrix, each encoded with a different value of γ (see appendix D). These manifold are dynamically retrieved by the network at different speeds, depending on the corresponding γ.
claims.evidence: Result from simulations shown in Figure 7(b).

claims.claim: The model allows simultaneous storage of memories without the constraint of a fixed dynamical timescale.
claims.source: This allows the model to simultaneously store memories without the constraint of a fixed dynamical timescale, an important feature for the description of biological circuits that need to be able to operate at different temporal scales.
claims.evidence: Inference from the model's capability to store manifolds with different speeds.

claims.claim: Different memories stored in the same neural population can interact with each other.
claims.source: Different memories stored in the same neural population can interact with each other, building more retrieval schemes in which, for example, the retrieval of a memory cues the retrieval of another one.
claims.evidence: Conceptual statement about model capabilities.

claims.claim: A mechanism for interaction between memories can result in sequential retrieval of multiple memories.
claims.source: To investigate this possibility, we have incorporated in the model a mechanism for interaction between memories, in which the endpoint of a dynamical, one-dimensional manifold elicits the activation of the start point of a different one (see Appendix E). This results in the sequential retrieval of multiple memories, one after the other, as illustrated in Figure 7 (d).
claims.evidence: Result from extended model shown in Figure 7(d).

claims.claim: The network retrieves manifolds in sequence, one at a time, following the instructed transitions encoded in its connectivity.
claims.source: The network retrieves the manifolds in sequence, one at a time, following the instructed transitions encoded in its connectivity.
claims.evidence: Description of behavior shown in Figure 7(d).

claims.claim: The all-or-nothing behavior of the coherence parameters segments the continuous dynamics into a sequence of discrete states.
claims.source: The all-or-nothing behavior of the coherence parameters segments the continuous dynamics of the network into a sequence of discrete states.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the results shown in Figure 7(d).

claims.claim: Within each retrieved manifold, the dynamic retains its continuous nature in the representation of the evolving position.
claims.source: Within each of the retrieved manifolds, the dynamic retains its continuous nature in the representation of the evolving position.
claims.evidence: Observation from Figure 7(d).

claims.claim: The sequential dynamic goes beyond simple cued retrieval and provides an example of a hybrid computational system encoding both continuous and discrete features.
claims.source: This sequential dynamic goes beyond the simple cued retrieval of independent memories that is the focus of most autoassociative memory models, and provides an example of a hybrid computational system, encoding both continuous and discrete features.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the model's capabilities.

claims.claim: The signal-to-noise approach involves writing the local field as the sum of a signal term from the retrieved map and a noise term from uncondensed maps.
claims.source: The signal-to-noise approach we follow, illustrated in details in Battaglia and Treves, 1998, involves writing the local field hi as the sum of two contributions: a signal term, due to the retrieved – 'condensed' – map, and a noise term consisting of the sum of the contributions of all the other, 'uncondensed' maps.
claims.evidence: Description of the analytical method, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The presence of asymmetry decreases the capacity but does not have a catastrophic effect.
claims.source: The presence of asymmetry decreases the capacity, but does not have a catastrophic effect: the decrease is continuous and scales with a power of γ.
claims.evidence: Result from analytical calculation shown in Figure 8(a).

claims.claim: There is a wide range of values of asymmetry and map sparsity in which a large number of dynamic manifolds can be stored and retrieved.
claims.source: There is therefore a wide range of values of asymmetry and map sparsity in which a large number of dynamic manifolds can be stored and retrieved.
claims.evidence: Conclusion from the capacity analysis.

claims.claim: A network with size in the order of ten thousand neurons could store from tens up to hundreds of dynamical memories.
claims.source: A network with size in the order of ten thousand neurons could store from tens up to hundreds of dynamical memories.
claims.evidence: Estimate based on capacity calculations shown in Figure 8(c).

claims.claim: The capacity for one dimensional attractors is higher than for two dimensional counterparts.
claims.source: The capacity for one dimensional attractors is higher than the one for their two dimensional counterparts. This is in line with what was found for symmetric networks (Battaglia and Treves, 1998).
claims.evidence: Result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 8(c), compared with previous work.

claims.claim: The peak of capacity is found for intermediate values of both map sparsity and the coefficient γ.
claims.source: Finally, we see that the peak of the capacity is found not only for intermediate values of map sparsity – again in line with what is known from the symmetric case – but also for intermediate values of the coefficient γ.
claims.evidence: Result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 8(c).

claims.claim: Moderate values of asymmetry can be beneficial for the storage of multiple continuous attractors.
claims.source: This shows that moderate values of asymmetry can be beneficial for the storage of multiple continuous attractors, a non-trivial phenomenon that may be crucial for the memory capacity of biological networks.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the capacity results.

claims.claim: The natural tendency of neural activity to show rich spontaneous dynamics does not hinder the possibility for multiple memories to coexist but can be crucial for correct memory functioning.
claims.source: In particular this suggests that the natural tendency of the neural activity to show a rich spontaneous dynamics not only does not hinder the possibility for multiple memories to coexist in the same population, but can be a crucial ingredient for the correct functioning of memory mechanisms.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the capacity results.

claims.claim: A continuous attractor neural network with memory-dependent asymmetric components can function as a dynamic memory.
claims.source: The results presented show how a continuous attractor neural network with memory-dependent asymmetric components in the connectivity can function as a dynamic memory.
claims.evidence: Summary of main results.

claims.claim: The model is simple enough to be treated analytically.
claims.source: Our model is simple enough to be treated analytically, robustly produces dynamic retrieval for a large range of the relevant parameters and shows a storage capacity that is comparable to – and in some cases higher than – the capacity for static continuous attractors.
claims.evidence: Summary of model properties.

claims.claim: The model robustly produces dynamic retrieval for a large range of relevant parameters.
claims.source: Our model is simple enough to be treated analytically, robustly produces dynamic retrieval for a large range of the relevant parameters and shows a storage capacity that is comparable to – and in some cases higher than – the capacity for static continuous attractors.
claims.evidence: Summary of model properties.

claims.claim: The model shows a storage capacity that is comparable to and in some cases higher than the capacity for static continuous attractors.
claims.source: Our model is simple enough to be treated analytically, robustly produces dynamic retrieval for a large range of the relevant parameters and shows a storage capacity that is comparable to – and in some cases higher than – the capacity for static continuous attractors.
claims.evidence: Summary of capacity results.

claims.claim: The analytical solution shows that the interaction between asymmetry strength and velocity of shift can be modulated by global features of network activity such as sparsity.
claims.source: The analytical solution of the single manifold case shows that the interaction between the strength of the asymmetry and the velocity of the shift can be modulated by global features of the network activity such as its sparsity.
claims.evidence: Result from analytical solution.

claims.claim: The network can retrieve at different velocities in different regimes without necessarily requiring short term synaptic modifications.
claims.source: This makes the network able to retrieve at different velocities in different regimes, without necessarily requiring short term synaptic modifications.
claims.evidence: Inference from the analytical results.

claims.claim: The model predicts that faster reactivations are to be expected in association with an increase in the excitability of the population.
claims.source: The dependence of the retrieval speed from the sparsity of the activity yields a testable prediction in the context of hippocampal replay: faster reactivations are to be expected in association with an increase in the excitability of the population.
claims.evidence: Prediction derived from the model.

claims.claim: The insensitivity of general features of dynamics to fine details of interaction shape suggests the mechanism could robustly emerge from learning or self-organization processes in the presence of noise.
claims.source: The insensitivity of the general features of the dynamics to the fine details of the shape of the interactions suggests that this mechanism could robustly emerge from learning or self organization processes in the presence of noise.
claims.evidence: Inference from robustness analysis.

claims.claim: The asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rule provides a simple and biologically realistic starting point for learning dynamic manifolds.
claims.source: The quantitative analysis of the learning process needed to effectively memorize low-dimensional dynamic manifolds is an interesting open direction, which goes beyond the scope of this work. However, the asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rule used here provides a simple and biologically realistic starting point.
claims.evidence: Statement about the biological plausibility of the mechanism.

claims.claim: The simple introduction of an asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rule is sufficient to describe a dynamic memory able to store and retrieve multiple manifolds with different speeds.
claims.source: Our analysis shows that the simple introduction of an aysmmetric Hebbian plasticity rule is sufficient to describe a dynamic memory able to store and retrieve multiple manifolds with different speeds, and it can incorporate interactions between them, producing the chained retrieval of a sequence of continuous memories.
claims.evidence: Summary of model capabilities.

claims.claim: The storage capacity for dynamic continuous attractors is large in magnitude and only mildly impacted by asymmetry in diluted networks.
claims.source: The central result of the paper is the quantification of the storage capacity for dynamic continuous attractors, that we find to be large in magnitude, only mildly impacted by the asymmetry in diluted networks, and even higher than the capacity for static attractors in fully connected networks with moderate degrees of asymmetry.
claims.evidence: Summary of capacity results.

claims.claim: The storage capacity for dynamic continuous attractors is higher than for static attractors in fully connected networks with moderate degrees of asymmetry.
claims.source: The central result of the paper is the quantification of the storage capacity for dynamic continuous attractors, that we find to be large in magnitude, only mildly impacted by the asymmetry in diluted networks, and even higher than the capacity for static attractors in fully connected networks with moderate degrees of asymmetry.
claims.evidence: Summary of capacity results.

claims.claim: Zhong et al., 2020 calculated the storage capacity of out of equilibrium continuous attractors in a different scenario with an external signal driving the activity bump.
claims.source: The storage capacity of out of equilibrium continuous attractors has been calculated, in a different scenario, by Zhong et al., 2020. The authors considered the case of an external signal driving the activity bump along the attractor, in a network of binary neurons, and proceeded to calculate the storage capacity with several assumptions that allowed to model the interference of multiple maps as thermal noise.
claims.evidence: Description of related work, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In the highly diluted regime, the velocity of the external signal has a mild detrimental effect on capacity according to Zhong et al., 2020.
claims.source: Interestingly, their main result is broadly compatible with what we show here: in the highly diluted regime the velocity of the external signal has a mild – detrimental – effect on the capacity.
claims.evidence: Comparison with results from Zhong et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Out of equilibrium effects could show some form of universality across different network models and implementations of the shift mechanism.
claims.source: This hints that out of equilibrium effects could show some form of universality across different network models and implementations of the shift mechanism.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on comparison with other work.

claims.claim: High capacity for dynamical sequences is achievable also in the case of discrete items according to Gillett et al., 2020.
claims.source: Moreover, a high capacity for dynamical sequences has shown to be achievable also in the case of discrete items (Gillett et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Statement supported by citation to Gillett et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The introduction of temporal structure is compatible with the functioning of autoassociative memory in recurrent networks.
claims.source: Together these results suggest that the introduction of a temporal structure is compatible with the functioning of autoassociative memory in recurrent networks, and they open the way to the use of attractor models for the quantitative analysis of complex memory phenomena, such as hippocampal replay and memory schemata.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple results.

claims.claim: The model suggests that the tendency of activity to move in the neural population is a natural feature of networks with asymmetric connectivity organized along a direction in a low dimensional manifold.
claims.source: The model we propose suggests that the tendency of the activity to move in the neural population is a natural feature of networks with asymmetric connectivity, when the asymmetry is organized along a direction in a low dimensional manifold, and that static memories could be the exception rather than the rule.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the model's implications.

claims.claim: Static memories could be the exception rather than the rule in networks with asymmetric connectivity.
claims.source: The model we propose suggests that the tendency of the activity to move in the neural population is a natural feature of networks with asymmetric connectivity, when the asymmetry is organized along a direction in a low dimensional manifold, and that static memories could be the exception rather than the rule.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on the model.

claims.claim: Mehta et al., 2000 showed that place fields can become more asymmetric in the course of spatial learning.
claims.source: Indeed, Mehta et al., 2000 have shown that place fields can become more asymmetric in the course of spatial learning, demonstrating that the idea that symmetry emerges from an averaging of trajectory-dependent effects (Sharp, 1991) does not always hold true.
claims.evidence: Statement supported by citations to Mehta et al., 2000 and Sharp, 1991.

claims.claim: The structural role of asymmetry has important implications for analysis methods that rely on assumptions of symmetry in interactions or equilibrium of neural activity.
claims.source: The structural role of the asymmetry has important implications for the analysis methods used to describe the activity of large populations of neurons, which often rely on the assumption of symmetry in the interactions (e.g. in the analysis of pairwise correlations) or equilibrium of the neural activity (e.g. the standard inverse Ising inference).
claims.evidence: Implication for experimental and analytical methods.

claims.claim: A progressive elongation of place fields in the running direction has been observed in rats running on a linear track.
claims.source: A progressive elongation of the place fields in the running direction has been observed in rats running on a linear track (Mehta et al., 1997), and our analysis predicts that an analogous effect would be observed also in open-field environments, when restricting the analysis to trajectories in the same running direction.
claims.evidence: Statement supported by citation to Mehta et al., 1997, with a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: The model predicts that an analogous elongation effect would be observed in open-field environments when restricting analysis to trajectories in the same running direction.
claims.source: A progressive elongation of the place fields in the running direction has been observed in rats running on a linear track (Mehta et al., 1997), and our analysis predicts that an analogous effect would be observed also in open-field environments, when restricting the analysis to trajectories in the same running direction.
claims.evidence: Prediction from the model.

claims.claim: Replayed sequences can be organized both forward and backward in time according to Foster and Wilson, 2006.
claims.source: Another challenge is posed by the evidence that replayed sequences can be organized both forward and backward in time (Foster and Wilson, 2006).
claims.evidence: Statement supported by citation to Foster and Wilson, 2006.

claims.claim: The model in its current formulation can produce retrieval of a sequence either forward or backward but cannot alternate between the two.
claims.source: The model in its current formulation can produce the retrieval of a given sequence either forward or backward, but cannot alternate between the two.
claims.evidence: Limitation of the current model.

claims.claim: If replay relies on asymmetric connections, the hippocampus would have to use different representations for forward and backward components.
claims.source: This suggests that, if replay relies on asymmetric connections, the hippocampus would have to use different representations for the forward and the backward component.
claims.evidence: Inference from the model's limitation.

claims.claim: A change in reward uniquely modulates backward replay according to Ambrose et al., 2016.
claims.source: The fact that a change in reward uniquely modulates backward replay (Ambrose et al., 2016) provides some evidence in this direction, but this question remains open to experimental investigation.
claims.evidence: Statement supported by citation to Ambrose et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The dynamical retrieval of the model generalizes the idea of cognitive maps by incorporating temporal organization in the low-dimensional manifold encoding memory structure.
claims.source: The dynamical retrieval of the model generalizes, in the framework of attractor networks, the idea of cognitive maps, incorporating a temporal organization in the low-dimensional manifold encoding the structure of the memory.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the model's contribution.

claims.claim: The dynamic nature of the model is reminiscent of memory schemata that guide and constrain mental activity.
claims.source: This feature is reminiscent of the idea of memory schemata – constructs that can guide and constrain our mental activity when we reminisce about the past, imagine future or fictional scenarios or let our minds free to wander (Ciaramelli and Treves, 2019).
claims.evidence: Comparison with memory schemata concept, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Using the model to describe memory schemata will require further steps such as accounting for hippocampus-neocortex interaction and expanding the mechanism for transitions between dynamical memories.
claims.source: The use of the present model to describe memory schemata will require further steps, such as an account of the interaction between hippocampus and neocortex, and the expansion of the mechanism describing the transition between different dynamical memories.
claims.evidence: Statement about future directions.

claims.claim: The idea of dynamic retrieval of a continuous manifold and integration with effective models of cortical memory networks open promising perspectives.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the idea of dynamic retrieval of a continuous manifold and the integration of the model presented here with effective models of cortical memory networks (Boboeva et al., 2018) open promising perspectives.
claims.evidence: Statement about future directions, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The full analytical description of a densely connected asymmetric attractor network is a challenge that remains open.
claims.source: Finally, the full analytical description of a densely connected asymmetric attractor network is a challenge that remains open, and can yield valuable insights on the workings of the neural circuits underlying memory.
claims.evidence: Statement about open challenges.

results.result: The authors introduce a continuous attractor network model with memory-dependent asymmetric synaptic connectivity that spontaneously breaks equilibrium and produces dynamic retrieval. The model is analytically tractable and robustly retrieves multiple dynamical memories across a wide range of parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C49, C69, C132-134 collectively establish the core model and its capabilities. The model is supported by both analytical derivations (C88, C133) and numerical simulations (C70-71, C93-95) showing robust dynamic retrieval. The biological motivation via STDP (C50, C61-62) provides plausibility, though actual learning dynamics are not demonstrated.

results.result: Asymmetric connectivity generates a steady flow of activity along the manifold direction without loss of coherence. The activity bump shifts at a speed that increases with asymmetry strength γ, as demonstrated in 1D, 2D, and 3D manifolds (Figure 2).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-75 describe the fundamental dynamic mechanism with direct support from simulations (Figure 2). The coherence preservation (C73) and speed dependence on γ (C75) are clearly demonstrated. The mechanism is shown to work across different dimensionalities, providing strong evidence for the core dynamics.

results.result: The model predicts that retrieval speed depends on both asymmetry strength γ and activity sparsity f, allowing the network to retrieve at different velocities without requiring short-term synaptic modifications. This yields a testable prediction that faster hippocampal replay should correlate with increased population excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C136-138 present a key prediction supported by analytical solutions (C136) and simulations (Figure 2d, Figure 3c). The functional relationship s(γ,f) is demonstrated empirically, though the exact form remains approximated. The prediction is specific and testable, making it a strong contribution.

results.result: The model admits a full analytical solution using a generalization of the Battaglia and Treves (1998) framework. The solution shows that dynamic retrieval occurs for all values of γ and characterizes how γ influences retrieval speed and bump asymmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C90, C92 describe the analytical treatment with results shown in Figure 3. The analytical solution provides exact characterization of bump shapes and their dependence on parameters. The approach is mathematically sound and provides theoretical foundation for the numerical observations.

results.result: Dynamic retrieval is robust across four orders of magnitude in both γ and ξ parameters. All features vary gradually with parameters, and the mechanism does not require fine-tuning, though it relies on exponential kernel shape.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-96 establish robustness through systematic parameter exploration (Figure 4). The wide parameter range and gradual variation support the robustness claim. However, C96 acknowledges dependence on exponential kernel form, which is then addressed by C97-99 showing robustness to kernel shape.

results.result: The dynamic retrieval mechanism is robust to the precise shape of the asymmetric kernel. Simulations with Gaussian-derivative, sinusoidal, and step-function kernels all produce stable shifting bumps, with only minor effects on bump shape details.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-99 demonstrate kernel-shape robustness through systematic testing (Figure 5). Three qualitatively different kernel shapes all produce the same fundamental dynamics. This addresses a potential limitation from C96 and strengthens the generality of the mechanism.

results.result: The network can store and retrieve multiple manifolds as an autoassociative memory. Given an initial configuration, it converges to the nearest attractor and moves along it, while activity projected on unretrieved manifolds appears as noise. Simulated recordings show sequential activity patterns only when sorted by the retrieved manifold.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-106 establish multi-memory capability with clear evidence from Figure 6. The selective retrieval (C103-104) and manifold-specific sequential patterns (C105-106) demonstrate proper memory function. The simulated electrophysiology (C105-106) provides a concrete link to experimental observations.

results.result: Multiple dynamic manifolds can be stored with different retrieval speeds by encoding each with a different γ value. This allows simultaneous storage of memories without constraint to a fixed dynamical timescale.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-109 demonstrate speed-multiplexing capability (Figure 7a-b). Five manifolds with different γ values are successfully retrieved at their respective speeds. This is a natural extension of the single-manifold results and is well-supported by simulations.

results.result: Memories can interact through a mechanism where manifold endpoints cue retrieval of other manifolds, producing sequential chained retrieval. This creates a hybrid system with discrete transitions between manifolds and continuous dynamics within each manifold.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-115 present the memory-chaining mechanism (Figure 7c-d). The sequential retrieval with all-or-nothing overlap dynamics (C113) and continuous within-manifold position (C114) is clearly demonstrated. However, the interaction mechanism is described only briefly in Appendix E, limiting full evaluation of its generality.

results.result: In diluted networks, asymmetry decreases storage capacity continuously (scaling with γ²) but not catastrophically. A wide range of γ and map sparsity values support storage of many dynamic manifolds.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-126, C142 present analytical capacity results (Figure 8a). The signal-to-noise analysis (C121) provides theoretical foundation. The continuous, non-catastrophic decrease with γ is clearly shown, and the capacity remains substantial across parameter ranges. The analytical approach is appropriate for the diluted regime.

results.result: In fully connected networks, a network of ~10,000 neurons can store tens to hundreds of dynamical memories. Capacity peaks at intermediate values of both map sparsity and γ, with moderate asymmetry actually enhancing capacity compared to static attractors.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-130, C143 present numerical capacity estimates (Figure 8b-c). The non-monotonic dependence on γ (C129-130) is a surprising and important finding. The capacity enhancement at intermediate γ (C143) is clearly demonstrated. The numerical approach is appropriate for the fully connected case where analytical methods are intractable.

results.result: At trajectory intersections in 2D manifolds, the network switches trajectories at low γ but successfully crosses at sufficiently high γ. Successful crossing requires the activity bump to be sufficiently elongated in the retrieval direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-84, C86 address trajectory crossing (Figure 2e). The γ-dependent transition from switching to crossing is demonstrated, and the dependence on ξ is characterized. The interpretation via bump elongation (C86) is intuitive and consistent with the mechanism. However, this is a limited exploration of position-dependent asymmetry.

results.result: The symmetric interaction kernel in continuous attractor networks arises from time-averaged Hebbian plasticity, but this neglects temporal structure. STDP can produce asymmetry when neurons fire sequentially along trajectories, as the postsynaptic neuron must fire after the presynaptic one for potentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C60-62 provide biological motivation for the asymmetric connectivity. The STDP mechanism (C62) is well-established (Markram et al., 1997), and the reasoning for how sequential firing produces asymmetry is sound. However, no learning simulations are performed to demonstrate this mechanism actually produces the required connectivity pattern.

results.result: The parameter γ regulates the relative strength of symmetric and asymmetric connectivity components. Asymmetric mechanisms have been shown to produce rigid shifts along manifolds without loss of coherence.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C66 describe model parameters and cite prior work (Zhang 1996, Burak & Fiete 2009, Fuhs & Touretzky 2006) establishing that asymmetric connectivity can produce coherent shifts. These are well-established results that provide foundation for the current work.

results.result: The robustness to interaction details suggests the mechanism could emerge from noisy learning processes. The asymmetric Hebbian rule provides a biologically realistic starting point, and is sufficient to describe dynamic memory with multiple manifolds at different speeds and inter-memory interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-141 make inferences about learning and biological plausibility. While the robustness results (C97-99) support C139's speculation, no actual learning simulations are performed. C140 acknowledges learning analysis is beyond scope. The claims are reasonable extrapolations but lack direct empirical support within this work.

results.result: The capacity results are compatible with Zhong et al. (2020) who found mild detrimental effects of velocity in a different out-of-equilibrium scenario, suggesting possible universality. High capacity for dynamical sequences is also achievable with discrete items (Gillett et al. 2020), indicating temporal structure is compatible with autoassociative memory function.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-148 compare results with related work. The comparison with Zhong et al. (2020) is appropriate and the compatibility is accurately stated. The speculation about universality (C146) is reasonable but tentative. The broader conclusion (C148) about compatibility of temporal structure with memory is well-supported by the convergent evidence.

results.result: The model suggests dynamic activity is a natural feature of asymmetric networks, with static memories potentially being exceptional. Mehta et al. (2000) showed place fields become more asymmetric during learning, supporting this view. The structural role of asymmetry has implications for analysis methods assuming symmetry or equilibrium.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-150 are speculative interpretations (marked as SPECULATION in evidence). C151 correctly cites supporting evidence, but this is a single study. C152's implications for analysis methods are reasonable but not demonstrated. These are interesting hypotheses but go beyond what the model directly establishes.

results.result: Place field elongation in the running direction has been observed on linear tracks (Mehta et al. 1997). The model predicts analogous elongation in open fields when analyzing trajectories in the same direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-154 present a testable prediction based on the model's bump asymmetry. The prediction is a logical extension of the linear track observations to 2D environments. The prediction is specific and experimentally testable, though not yet validated.

results.result: Replayed sequences can be forward or backward (Foster & Wilson 2006), but the current model cannot alternate between directions. This suggests the hippocampus might use different representations for forward and backward components, with some support from reward modulation of backward replay (Ambrose et al. 2016).
results.evaluation: Claims C155-158 identify a model limitation and speculate about solutions. C156 correctly identifies the limitation. C157's speculation about separate representations is reasonable but undemonstrated. C158 cites relevant evidence but acknowledges the question remains open. This is an honest assessment of limitations but the proposed solution is speculative.

results.result: The model generalizes cognitive maps by incorporating temporal organization in memory manifolds, reminiscent of memory schemata. Application to schemata would require accounting for hippocampus-neocortex interaction and expanded transition mechanisms, but the dynamic retrieval concept and integration with cortical models offer promising perspectives.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-162 discuss potential applications to memory schemata. The connection is conceptually reasonable (C160 cites Ciaramelli & Treves 2019) but C161 acknowledges substantial additional work is needed. These are speculative future directions rather than established results, though the speculation is well-grounded in the demonstrated capabilities.

results.result: The introduction establishes that episodic memory has dynamic temporal structure, exemplified by hippocampal replay, preplay, and sequences in various contexts. Similar dynamics appear in memory schemata and motor programs. Most existing models treat memories as static, while computational analyses of dynamics don't focus on memory storage. The concept of dynamical continuous attractors involves activity constrained to and moving along low-dimensional manifolds.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-48 provide background and motivation, extensively citing prior work. The characterization of existing models (C3, C39-40) and the gap they address is accurate. The biological phenomena (C2, C9-28) are well-documented in cited literature. The conceptual framework (C33-35) is clearly defined. This effectively motivates the work, though these are primarily literature review claims.

results.result: The signal-to-noise analytical approach involves decomposing the local field into a signal term from the retrieved map and a noise term from uncondensed maps, following Battaglia and Treves (1998).
results.evaluation: Claim C121 describes the analytical method with appropriate citation. This is a standard approach for analyzing diluted attractor networks and is correctly applied here. The method is well-established and appropriate for the problem.

results.result: The natural tendency of neural activity to show rich spontaneous dynamics not only doesn't hinder memory coexistence but can be crucial for correct memory functioning.
results.evaluation: Claim C131 is marked as INFERENCE and SPECULATION. While the capacity results (C129-130) show moderate asymmetry can enhance capacity, the stronger claim that dynamics are "crucial" for memory function goes beyond the demonstrated results. The capacity is still substantial even without asymmetry (γ=0), so dynamics appear beneficial but not strictly necessary.

results.result: Full analytical description of densely connected asymmetric attractor networks remains an open challenge that could yield valuable insights.
results.evaluation: Claim C163 accurately identifies a limitation and future direction. The paper addresses this by using numerical simulations for the fully connected case (Figure 8b-c) while providing analytical results only for the diluted regime. This is an honest acknowledgment of the current state of the field.
